studies.label: Main online writing and post-editing experiment

counts_source.quote:
Following
our preregistered exclusion criteria, we discarded
responses where participants never edited any of
the LLM-generated drafts or did not complete the
entire study, leaving 81 participants.

arms.name: Post-edited LLM drafts
arms.description: Participants plan fictional details, receive an LLM-generated full draft, and edit it to express their personal style. Four randomly selected tasks per analyzed writer (PDF pp. 4-5, section 4; PDF p. 24, Table 9).

arms.name: Unassisted human writing
arms.description: The same participants plan details and write directly from those plans without seeing LLM-generated text. Two randomly selected tasks per analyzed writer (PDF pp. 4-5, section 4; PDF p. 24, Table 9).

studies.task: Writers choose personal writing scenarios, such as letters, speeches, vows, or tributes, plan fictional content, and either post-edit an AI draft or write unaided to convey their own style (PDF pp. 4-5 and 24).

ai_tool.name: GPT-o4-mini
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 5, section 5.1: "LLM drafts were generated using GPT-o4-mini (OpenAI, 2025)."

preregistration.where: https://aspredicted.org/ck6xk4.pdf, linked in PDF p. 1, footnote 2; the paper’s hypothesis description is on PDF p. 3, Section 3. The registry document was not separately consulted.
preregistration.primary_outcome: The paper describes stylistic authenticity (H1) and stylistic homogeneity (H2) as its two main preregistered hypotheses. It does not designate a unique primary endpoint. H2a compares homogeneity in post-edited and unassisted writing.

estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine similarity between LUAR-MUD style embeddings of texts written by different participants, computed separately within the post-edited and unassisted conditions. Higher similarity means greater stylistic homogeneity and less diversity (PDF pp. 5-7, sections 5.2 and 6.2, Figure 6; PDF p. 16, Appendix B.2).

sources.quote:
Each of the 81 partic-
ipants chose six tasks to complete. Four were randomly
selected as treatment and two as control.

We see that post-edited writing is indeed more
stylistically homogeneous than unassisted writing
(H2a, p = .0002, g = 1.42, 95% CI: [1.33, 1.51])

with corresponding effect sizes reported as Hedges’
g (Hedges, 1981) with 95% confidence intervals
calculated from 1000 bootstrap samples.

estimates.notes: Independent reconciliation checked the analyzed counts, outcome definition, unit, AI availability, direction, and repeated-participant design against the PDF. Each retained writer completed both randomized blocks, so n_treatment and n_control refer to the same people and n_total counts each person once (PDF p. 24, Table 9). The paper prints no first-round-only result; within_person=paired describes the complete repeated-participant comparison, without asserting that the analysis preserved pairing. The supplied AI draft remained available while the treatment output was produced (PDF p. 5, section 4). The unassisted block is the randomized comparator in the same session; no separate after-AI assessment is reported. Section 6 specifies permutation tests and bootstrap intervals (PDF p. 5); Appendix A.2 describes permutations of similarity scores (PDF pp. 13-14), but the resampling unit and handling of repeated writers are not established for these contrasts. Retain se_basis=unclear. No numerical permutation statistic is printed, so stats.test is null; the test method is documented here. The standardizing SD for Hedges’ g is not defined. The recorded interval is for g, not a raw mean difference. No raw arm means, arm SDs/SEs, raw differences or raw-scale uncertainty are printed. No statistic was calculated or estimated from a plot. The contrast compares stylistic similarity among different writers within each assigned writing condition, so question=across_people, construct=diversity, and unit=pair (PDF pp. 6-7, section 6.2 and Figure 6). Higher cosine similarity means more homogeneous writing; higher_is=more_similar. The positive printed g therefore indicates less diversity with AI. The number of analyzed pairs is not printed and remains null. Figure 6 supplies distributions without numerical arm means. H2a is part of the main preregistered H2 hypothesis as described in the paper (PDF p. 3); the registry document was not separately consulted. LUAR-MUD is the selected main embedding model (PDF p. 16, Appendix B.2).

estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine similarity between CISR style embeddings of texts written by different participants, repeating the H2a comparison of post-edited and unassisted writing with an alternative embedding model (PDF p. 16, Appendix B.2 and Table 3). The comparison uses the between-writer text-pair measure defined in section 6.2 and Figure 6 (PDF pp. 6-7); higher values mean more similar writing.

estimates.outcome: Linguistic acceptability of final writing (CoLA score)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Model-judged linguistic acceptability using the Morris et al. model fine-tuned on expert human judgments from the Corpus of Linguistic Acceptability (CoLA). Applied to all control, generated, and post-edited texts; the extracted contrast compares post-edited with unassisted writing (PDF p. 21, Appendix B.7.1). Figure 12 (PDF p. 20) labels higher scores as more acceptable. This is a narrow measure of language quality of personal creative writing, not an expert creativity rating.

estimates.notes: Independent reconciliation checked the analyzed counts, outcome definition, unit, AI availability, direction, and repeated-participant design against the PDF. Each retained writer completed both randomized blocks, so n_treatment and n_control refer to the same people and n_total counts each person once (PDF p. 24, Table 9). The paper prints no first-round-only result; within_person=paired describes the complete repeated-participant comparison, without asserting that the analysis preserved pairing. The supplied AI draft remained available while the treatment output was produced (PDF p. 5, section 4). The unassisted block is the randomized comparator in the same session; no separate after-AI assessment is reported. Section 6 specifies permutation tests and bootstrap intervals (PDF p. 5); Appendix A.2 describes permutations of similarity scores (PDF pp. 13-14), but the resampling unit and handling of repeated writers are not established for these contrasts. Retain se_basis=unclear. No numerical permutation statistic is printed, so stats.test is null; the test method is documented here. The standardizing SD for Hedges’ g is not defined. The recorded interval is for g, not a raw mean difference. No raw arm means, arm SDs/SEs, raw differences or raw-scale uncertainty are printed. No statistic was calculated or estimated from a plot. This exploratory measure scores linguistic quality of individual personal-writing outputs, so question=with_ai, construct=usefulness, measure=automated_score, and unit=output (PDF pp. 20-21, Figure 12 and Appendix B.7.1). It is not an argumentative or expository writing-proficiency composite. higher_is=other means greater linguistic acceptability, as explicitly labeled in Figure 12; the score does not directly measure creativity or originality. The prose says post-edited text is more acceptable than unassisted control text, but its printed g and interval are negative. The subtraction order is not stated. The negative effect and interval are retained exactly as printed on PDF p. 21, without reversing their signs or treating them as treatment minus control. This orientation must be resolved before calculating a signed AI-assistance effect. Figure 12 prints no numerical arm means. The total number of scored outputs is not printed for this analysis; it has not been computed from task counts. The model was trained on expert judgments, but these study outputs were scored by the model, not by expert raters.

not_extracted.what: S1-O1, H2b: post-edited versus original LLM-generated stylistic homogeneity (LUAR-MUD and CISR)
not_extracted.reason: The original unedited drafts are a model-generated reference stage, not an independently assigned human comparison arm. This before/after editing contrast does not estimate randomized AI assistance versus unassisted work or another human AI configuration (PDF p. 6, Section 6.2; p. 7, Figure 6; p. 16, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: S1-O2, H2c: similarity to other participants’ post-edited texts versus own unassisted texts (LUAR-MUD and CISR)
not_extracted.reason: The scored post-edited texts are held fixed and the reference source changes. This is a reference-source diagnostic, not a contrast between the randomized writing conditions (PDF p. 6, Section 6.2 and Figure 5; p. 16, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: S1-O3, H1a: stylistic similarity to own unassisted writing before versus after editing (LUAR-MUD and CISR)
not_extracted.reason: The contrast compares an original model-generated draft with its human-post-edited version. The unassisted human text is only a fixed reference; the statistic does not compare AI-assisted and unassisted human outputs as treatment and control (PDF p. 5, Section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3; p. 16, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: S1-O4, H1a-prime: similarity of the same post-edited text to own versus others’ unassisted writing (LUAR-MUD and CISR)
not_extracted.reason: This is an output-based diversity diagnostic under the screening form, but it changes the reference author rather than the randomized aid condition. It supplies no additional randomized assistance contrast (PDF p. 6, Section 6.1 and Figure 5; p. 16, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: S1-O5, H1b: similarity to LLM-generated text and Pangram AI-authorship likelihood before versus after editing
not_extracted.reason: LUAR-MUD, CISR, and Pangram compare original model-generated drafts with post-edited drafts. They do not report a full-sample contrast of the assigned post-editing and unassisted human-writing conditions on this outcome (PDF p. 5, Section 6.1; p. 6, Figure 3; p. 16, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: S1-O6, H1c: similarity of post-edited texts to own unassisted style versus LLM style (LUAR-MUD and CISR)
not_extracted.reason: The same AI-assisted output is scored against two reference sources; these are not two assigned human aid conditions. The observed reference-source gap is not an AI-assistance effect (PDF p. 6, Section 6.1 and Figure 4; p. 16, Table 3).

not_extracted.what: S1-O7: CoLA linguistic acceptability, post-edited versus original LLM-generated drafts
not_extracted.reason: The original LLM draft is a model-generated reference stage, not a human comparison arm. Only the separately reported post-edited-versus-unassisted-human contrast is extracted (PDF pp. 20-21, Figure 12 and Appendix B.7.1).

not_extracted.what: S1: perceived stylistic self-similarity and authenticity of own text
not_extracted.reason: Participants rated how well the texts captured their own style; these are excluded self-reports, including the post-edited-versus-control and post-edited-versus-original-draft comparisons (PDF pp. 7-8, Sections 6.3 and 6.5; Figure 7; p. 29, Figure 21).

not_extracted.what: S1, H3: correlation of perceived stylistic similarity with LUAR-measured similarity
not_extracted.reason: A correlation involving participant self-reports is not a randomized between-condition effect on produced output (PDF p. 7, Section 6.3 and Figure 8).

not_extracted.what: S1: perceived usability / willingness to use the written text, including H4
not_extracted.reason: Self-reported willingness to use a text and its correlation with self-reported authenticity are excluded; no actual use behavior is measured (PDF p. 8, Section 6.5; pp. 16-17, Appendix B.3 and Figure 9; p. 29, Figure 21).

not_extracted.what: S1: willingness to use AI, confidence in ability to post-edit, and preferred future writing workflow
not_extracted.reason: These are attitudes, preferences, and pre/post self-reports, not creativity or diversity scored on participants’ outputs (PDF p. 8, Section 6.5; pp. 25-26, Figures 16 and 18).

not_extracted.what: S1: perceived mental demand, time, effort, frustration, and success in the writing tasks
not_extracted.reason: The task-difficulty survey measures self-reported workload and performance perceptions. The reported comparisons do not measure the creative quality of the text (PDF p. 8, Section 6.5; p. 25, Figure 17).

not_extracted.what: S1, H5: demographic differences in initial stylistic similarity and post-editing burden; desires to express or mask identity
not_extracted.reason: These are demographic subgroup comparisons, measurement correlations, or self-reported identity preferences, not full-sample randomized assistance contrasts (PDF pp. 17-18, Appendix B.4 and Figure 10).

not_extracted.what: S1: style-importance moderation models for H1a, H1b, and H1c (Tables 4-6)
not_extracted.reason: The models test moderation by perceived style importance, and their conditional editing or reference-source coefficients are not full-sample randomized aid effects. Table 6 also leaves its same-participant predictor coding inconsistent with the caption’s reference-source description (PDF pp. 18-19, Appendix B.5).

not_extracted.what: S1-O3/S1-O4: mixed-effects model linking changes in linguistic acceptability to changes in stylistic similarity (Table 8)
not_extracted.reason: This is an association/moderation analysis adjusted for CoLA-score change, a post-treatment variable. Its reference-author coefficient also compares reference sources rather than assigned aid conditions (PDF p. 21, Appendix B.7.1 and Table 8).

not_extracted.what: S1: consistency of original LLM-generated style for the same versus different participants
not_extracted.reason: This analysis checks model-generated drafts before human editing, not the effects of assistance on completed human work (PDF p. 14, Appendix B.1).

not_extracted.what: S1: authorship-identification MRR and recall benchmarks for the candidate style-embedding models
not_extracted.reason: These are model-validation results on control texts, not a human AI-assistance contrast or a convergent test completed by participants (PDF pp. 14-16, Appendix B.2 and Table 2).

not_extracted.what: S1: rankings of originality, privacy, overall quality, style, ownership, efficiency, and reliability as reasons for future workflow preference
not_extracted.reason: These self-reported priorities compare groups defined by their own preferences. Originality and quality here refer to reasons for liking AI drafts, not independently scored creativity of participants’ outputs (PDF pp. 19-20, Appendix B.6, Table 7 and Figure 11).

not_extracted.what: S1: contractions, LLM-associated words, punctuation/em-dash removals, and total word-volume comparisons
not_extracted.reason: These describe original model output and changes during post-editing. The appendix does not report a full-sample post-edited-versus-unassisted human contrast on these text features; original-generation-versus-control comparisons include an unedited model-only benchmark (PDF pp. 21-22, Appendix B.7.2).

not_extracted.what: S1: number, length, and total character volume of edited spans and their correlations with self-similarity change
not_extracted.reason: These are within-treatment descriptions and observational associations of editing behavior, not randomized assistance contrasts (PDF p. 22, Appendix B.7.3 and Figure 13).

not_extracted.what: S1: individual example changes in similarity, Pangram score, word error rate, and punctuation; selected qualitative editing cases
not_extracted.reason: The examples and manually selected cases are not full-sample condition contrasts (PDF pp. 7-8, Section 6.4; p. 15, Table 1; pp. 20-21, Appendix B.7.1).

not_extracted.what: S2: separate formative scenario-selection survey and personal-style importance ratings
not_extracted.reason: Only scenario presentation order was randomized. Respondents received no AI assistance and produced no scored creative output. The formative respondents were excluded from the main study sample (PDF pp. 22-24, Appendix C and Figures 14-15).

open_items: The paper reports recruitment and the retained sample, but not an explicit assignment-stage participant count, block-sequence counts, allocation algorithm, or the timing and breakdown of exclusions (PDF pp. 4, 13, and 24).
No first-round-only results or counts are printed. All extracted contrasts use both randomized blocks from the same writers; potential carryover cannot be separated from these printed results.

Neither diversity measure has printed arm means, SDs/SEs, a raw cosine-similarity difference or raw-scale interval, or an exact number of analyzed text pairs. Only standardized effects and their intervals can be transcribed (PDF pp. 6-7 and 16).
The CoLA analysis lacks printed arm means, SDs/SEs, and the number of analyzed outputs; the paper does not specify whether any within-writer aggregation preceded its test (PDF pp. 20-21).

The exact resampling units and handling of repeated outputs and pairs sharing writers are not established. Participant-valid uncertainty must not be assumed for any of the extracted contrasts (PDF p. 5, section 6; PDF pp. 13-14, Appendix A.2).
The paper does not specify the denominator or observation level used to standardize Hedges’ g. No SD, standard error, or raw-scale contrast has been derived from the printed effects or intervals.

The CoLA effect and confidence interval are negative as printed, while the prose says post-edited writing is more acceptable than unassisted writing. The subtraction order must be checked in labeled analysis inputs or code before assigning the effect a treatment-minus-control sign (PDF p. 21, Appendix B.7.1).
Participant country is not reported. The preregistration itself was not read, and preregistered primary status of the CISR robustness specification cannot be confirmed from the paper.
The citation record identifies a later proceedings publication. These estimates use the supplied local preprint; numerical equivalence to the later publication was not checked.

The screening form also flags uncertain units and reference aggregation for H2c, H1a-prime, H1b, and H1c; whether H1a-prime compares changes or final levels; and the inconsistent reference-source predictor label in Table 6. Those analyses are listed in not_extracted because they do not compare randomized human assistance conditions, or adjust for post-treatment variables. Their unresolved details do not require additional eligible estimates (PDF pp. 6, 13-14, 18-19, and 21).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-11 against the supplied arXiv PDF. The full markdown conversion was read consecutively through its end, including references and Appendices A-D. All cited pages were independently extracted with pymupdf, and Table 3 was checked against its PDF text and table extraction. All locators use one-based PDF file pages; this preprint has no separate printed page numbers. The supplied diff contains one flagged field disagreement and no estimates unique to either extractor. The reconciled file retains A’s slugs; wording differences in B’s slugs do not denote additional estimates. Additional checks reconciled null-versus-empty country, test-object representation, and the printed p-value bound. Agreement was independently checked for study and arm counts and for every retained estimate’s counts, question, construct, unit, higher_is, outcome_with_ai, and within_person. The study randomizes writing-block order and task allocation (PDF p. 4, section 4; PDF p. 24, Table 9). The recruitment count is not explicitly an assignment-stage count, so n_randomized remains null (PDF pp. 4 and 13). Participants are English-fluent Prolific users; country is not stated (PDF p. 13, Appendix A.1). The model supplies complete initial prose from participant-written content plans and the human then edits it, supporting ai_role=other (PDF pp. 4-5). Original LLM drafts are a reference stage, not a separate human comparison arm. Every screening-form outcome and contrast is either represented by an estimate or covered by not_extracted. No additional eligible outcome or contrast was found. The two H2a measurements share the same sample. The formative survey and main experiment used disjoint samples, and no overlap with another paper is stated (PDF p. 23, Appendix C). The saved preprint is the source for these numbers; the later proceedings publication identified by the citation record was not consulted. No external API, posted data, derived statistic, or figure-read value was used. Only extraction/c710.json was written.
